title: Half a Million Miles and Counting, This Volvo 142S Is Ready for Its Second Act

body_markdown:
Not long ago, we featured a 2006 Ford GT with just 8 miles on the odometer, which sold for an eye-opening[$2.1M](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/2-1-million-gets-you-a-museum-quality-2006-ford-gt-heritage/) . It wasn’t the first “wrapper car” we’ve covered, nor will it be the last. Ultra-low-mile cars are a thing, of course, and the market often celebrates them, while market observers—particularly those who populate comments sections—tend to wring their hands. “Cars are meant to be driven!” goes the common refrain. “Hold my[Norrlands Guld](https://www.beeradvocate.com/beer/profile/4087/22009/) !” comes the reply from[this 1971 Volvo 142S](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1970-volvo-142s-2/) . The 550,000-mile Swede sold this week for $6668, a rather unremarkable result for a remarkable car.


Volvo’s development of the 140 began in 1960, with a project internally dubbed P660. The mandate called for an entirely new car that could carry two-door coupe, four-door sedan, and five-door wagon bodies, and which offered improved safety features and more interior space than either the 120 “Amazon” series or[PV444/544](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/volvo/pv544/1965/1965-volvo-pv544-base?id=aCn1I000000DVM0SAO) , all while sharing the same 102-inch wheelbase that underpinned those models. Designer Jan Wilsgaard leaned on his personal motto, “simple is beautiful,” as he created a few different boxy, upright prototypes. By early 1964, he’d gotten the greenlight on the design that would become the 140.


Bring a Trailer/NMOldToys9


The car debuted August 17, 1966, as the four-door 144, with Volvo’s new nomenclature baked into the name: “1” for the series, “4” for the number of cylinders, “4” for the number doors. The rounded PV cars had just been discontinued, following a production run spanning two decades, and the Amazon was now in its tenth year, so much was riding on the new-look 140. Wilsgaard and Volvo could have had no idea it would become the carmaker’s first million-unit seller, while also defining the brick-like look of the company for the next 27 years.


[Safety features](https://www.hagerty.com/media/lists/10-fantastic-vintage-volvo-ads/) introduced on the 140 included a structural cage around the passengers, with front and rear crumple zones, a collapsible steering column, and four-wheel disc brakes on a dual-circuit system, which also featured two pressure-relief valves to help prevent lock-up during hard braking. Further innovations would find their way into the 140 series throughout its nine-year production run.

Bring a Trailer/NMOldToys9


Bring a Trailer/NMOldToys9


The 142 coupe arrived in 1967 and the 145 wagon a year later, and all were powered initially by the same 75-horsepower 1.8-liter B18 found in the Amazon, running through either a three-speed automatic or four-speed manual transmission. The sportier 144S trim utilized the more powerful B18B from the 123GT and P1800, with dual carbs and higher compression, good for 90 hp. For 1969, the 118-hp, twin-carb 2.0-liter B20 became the standard engine, with Bosch fuel injection entering the conversation for 1972.


Exterior changes were few, and not counting the protruding “commando” safety bumpers introduced for 1974, the most significant was the 1971 front end revision, which traded the split metal grille similar to that of the Amazon for a black one incorporating the diagonal slash we now associate with the brand.


Bring a Trailer/NMOldToys9


Bring a Trailer/NMOldToys9


Our feature car hit the road right in the middle of production, and the listing notes it was with its original New Mexico owner until 2023. Plenty of people have owned cars for that long; far fewer have driven them such distances. Given our collective attention span today, and the composition of so many new cars, it’s possible feats like that are a thing of the past.


Bring a Trailer/NMOldToys9


Bring a Trailer/NMOldToys9


The car presents in what can best be described as “shabby chic,” which isn’t a category in Hagerty Valuation Tools but is best approximated by something like a #5—[a little south of “fair.”](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/volvo/142s/1970/1970-volvo-142s-base?id=aCn1I000000DPnRSAW) But really, after the equivalent of 22 trips around the Earth, how might any car look? The original Safari Yellow paint is decent enough, shiny in some places and not shiny in others, with a few spots of light corrosion in and around the wheel wells. There are a couple spots of more serious (but not *so* serious) rust in the floorpans. The dash shows a crack or two—far fewer than many equivalent (and many newer) New Mexico cars do. The interior, in fact, looks pretty darn good, though the headliner is tired. Who isn’t?


The B20 was reportedly rebuilt at some point, its Stromberg carbs changed out for dual SUs in the process, though the originals are included. The original four-speed transmission, too, was swapped for an M41 four-speed with overdrive, all of which makes the car a bit more cruise-friendly.


As one commenter noted after the sale concluded, “This car is so much more interesting to me than supercars, muscle cars, and modified vehicles.” I’m sure they’re not alone. We talk in this hobby about “honest cars,” and this 1970 Volvo 142S is about as upstanding as they come. Kinda tired, somewhat dingy—it’s seen some things. With a fresh set of tires and a weekend once-over, who here doubts it’ll be ready to see more things? Cars *are* meant to be driven, and none of us should be surprised when this one hits a million miles.
